params.notes: This is the problem the benchmark addresses. Most benchmark scores ask whether the model produced the right answer and report a single number. In a clinic, the deliverable is judged three other ways. First, in physical units: a registration of the pre-operative MRI to the ultrasound is only useful if landmarks line up within about 2 millimetres; an organ mask matters because of the volume in millilitres; a risk score has to be calibrated, meaning a predicted 20 % risk should come true about 20 % of the time. Second, in time: a pipeline that needs an hour per scan cannot be used during surgery. Third, against a specialist: the fair bar is the dedicated system a hospital would use, run on the same hidden cases, not a leaderboard from another dataset. Transition: so we built tasks that measure all three.
params.title: Clinical evaluation — what a generic benchmark score leaves out

params.notes: Here is how every task works, left to right. The agent, Claude Code with web tools removed, gets a workspace with a clinical README, development cases with their reference answers, and network access only to the model API. It has 30 to 60 minutes. What it must leave behind is not an answer but a pipeline: a run.sh that takes an input folder and writes the clinical output, offline. A separate verifier, which the agent never sees, runs that pipeline on hidden cases under a clinical time limit, scores the output in clinical units, and compares it with a specialist system's stored outputs on the very same cases. The seven families span imaging, signals and statistics: registering brain MRI to intra-operative ultrasound, a CT spleen mask with its volume, fetal head circumference from ultrasound, retinal vessel segmentation judged against a second human reader, a calibrated ECG classifier, ICU mortality risk, and a treatment-effect estimate with a confidence interval. The last three turned out to be controls: tasks both the specialist and the agents pass, which shows the harness is not simply too hard. Two more families were built and excluded because no comparator could pass their bar; they are in the backup. Transition: here is how the two frontier models did across three attempts each.

params.notes: A new task this round: segment the blood vessels in 8 hidden retinal photographs of children's eyes. The bar on each image is set by a second human expert: the pipeline must agree with the first expert at least as well as the second expert did, on two measures. Dice is plain overlap; clDice, centreline Dice, checks whether thin vessels stay connected. In the chart, each column is one hidden image; the short black tick is the second expert's score, which is the bar; the diamond is the specialist and the dots are the agents. Hollow means that image failed. Both agents trained a small U-Net from scratch on the 20 development images, on a CPU, in about 20 to 35 minutes. On average their overlap is higher than the second human's, 0.83 against 0.78. Opus passes 5 of 8 images, Sonnet 4 of 8, against 6 of 8 for a specialist trained on a GPU. On the two hardest images, which the specialist also fails, they miss on both measures; on the six the specialist passes, every miss is on connectivity, by less than 0.02. So this is near-parity, not a demonstrated gap; with 6 images the specialist passes, we could only show a gap if an agent failed at least 3 of them. Transition: the limits of all this.

params.notes: Be direct about the limits. Three attempts per task and model is better than one, but it is not a variance estimate, and the spread is large: the same model on the same fetal head task scored anywhere from 0.42 to 0.86. Registration, spleen and vessels have only six to eight hidden cases, so 'no gap shown' there means not enough data, not proof of parity. The hosted agent ran at Claude Code's default effort, not high. Valkyrie does not keep our grader's detailed metrics file, so raw millimetre and Dice values come from regrading each saved pipeline locally; those regrades match every hosted reward key in 28 of 30 headline attempts, and the two exceptions are explained in the README. All data are public, so contamination is possible; we saw no recalled labels and no web use. On the right is how anyone can rerun it on Valkyrie: push the no-web Claude Code agent, start a run on the dataset. Everything, including every run ID, is in the README. params.notes: The exact gap rule and every verdict. For the per-case tasks we take only the hidden cases the specialist passes, called S, and compute agent minus specialist pass rate with a paired bootstrap interval. A gap is claimed only when the agent fails at least one of those cases and the whole interval is below zero. Fetal head shows a gap in all six attempts, with intervals far from zero. Registration and spleen have S of 4 and 3, so a gap can only be shown when an agent fails most of them; 'no gap shown' there means the interval reaches zero, which is underpowered rather than reassuring. For ECG and ICU, the cohort rule applies: a gap if the agent misses a gate part the specialist meets. Opus missed the heart-attack sensitivity part once, at 0.693 against 0.70.

params.notes: Where this project started. The original question was whether frontier models can predict gene mutations in primary central nervous system lymphoma from MRI features. On the public UCSF release, 64 patients with genetic records and 439 imaging features, no method gave reliable evidence of signal: AUROC, where 0.5 is a coin flip, stayed near or below 0.5 for TabPFN, a strong tabular model, and for GPT-5.2; a simple logistic model reached 0.56 for MYD88 with a permutation p-value of 0.27. The one higher number, 0.67 for a ten-feature model, is a descriptive internal cross-validation without a confidence interval. If nothing passes, a failure by frontier models cannot be told apart from a task that is impossible with these data. So we moved to tasks where a specialist provably succeeds, which is the design of this suite. All patient-level data stayed on UCSF servers.
params.title: PCNSL mutation prediction — no method above chance

params.notes: How the datasets were chosen. The survey rated 50 candidate entries, some of them variants of one source, in four steps. First the licence: the task image is uploaded to a commercial platform, so the data must allow redistribution, which means CC BY, CC BY-SA or ODC-By; anything non-commercial or no-derivatives is out. Second, a clinical measure with a published bar. Third, a specialist that actually passes that bar on our hidden cases. Fourth, a size that fits in a task image. Most of the datasets from Jin's course material failed at the first step: the skin-lesion set HAM10000 is non-commercial, the APTOS retina set is under Kaggle's competition rules, the Open-i chest X-ray reports are non-commercial no-derivatives, and the DRIVE and STARE vessel sets state no licence at all. That is why the vessel task uses CHASE_DB1, which is CC BY.
params.title: Dataset selection — licence, clinical bar, specialist, size

params.notes: Where each clinical bar comes from. Registration and spleen bars come from published clinical accuracy and inter-observer studies; the fetal head tolerance is the inter-observer limit between sonographers; the vessel bar is a second human expert's own agreement on each image; the ECG heart-attack operating point comes from the classic CSE study; the ICU bar is the challenge's own score against the SAPS-I baseline; the treatment-effect gate follows the published analysis of the 2016 causal inference competition. Where no published number existed, for example the 90 % family bar or the calibration bounds, we declared our own convention before any agent ran and say so.
